passages.text: Underwater Tunnels Explained: How Engineers Build Tunnels Beneath Rivers and Seas Published on 25 November, 2026 | Updated on 25 November, 2026 Introduction Underwater tunnels are remarkable examples of modern civil engineering. They allow roads, railways, pedestrians and utility services to pass beneath rivers, lakes and seas without interrupting shipping or relying on bridges across the water. A common misconception is that underwater tunnels are built directly inside the water. In reality, most underwater crossings use one of two main construction methods. Some tunnels are excavated through soil or rock beneath the riverbed or seabed, while others are constructed from large prefabricated sections that are floated into position, lowered into a prepared trench and connected underwater. Both methods solve the same fundamental engineering challenge: creating a safe, stable and watertight passage while resisting groundwater pressure, soil loads and the surrounding geological conditions. The selection of a construction method depends on water depth, tunnel length, ground conditions, navigation requirements, environmental restrictions and project economics. Method 1: Bored Tunnels Beneath the Seabed or Riverbed A bored underwater tunnel passes through rock or soil below the bed of a river or sea. Engineers must consider groundwater pressure, structural loads, settlement, temperature changes, seismic effects where relevant and long-term durability. For bored tunnels, the stability of the excavation face and control of groundwater inflow are major concerns. Unexpected fractures or weak geological zones can cause water ingress and ground loss. For immersed tube tunnels, trench preparation, element positioning, joint sealing and settlement control are particularly important. Marine construction also introduces challenges from currents, tides, waves, weather and underwater visibility. Both systems require reliable drainage, ventilation, fire protection, emergency access and monitoring. Their operation and maintenance must be considered from the beginning of the design process. Conclusion Underwater tunnels usually pass beneath rivers and seas rather than directly through the water. Bored tunnels are excavated through suitable rock or soil using tunnelling equipment, while immersed tube tunnels are built from prefabricated sections that are floated, lowered into a prepared trench and connected underwater. The success of both methods depends on careful geological investigations, groundwater control, structural design, waterproofing and construction quality. passages.text: Tunnels can be constructed using various methods that depend on the materials used, the tunnel’s purpose, and its type. The most commonly used method involves building a tunnel on the ground and placing it underwater. Ships and ferries are vulnerable to high tides and storms that can easily swallow them. In 1954, five ferries were lost in the Tsugaru Strait, the body of water between Hokkaido Island and Aomori Prefecture, due to typhoons. The public was outraged; building a bridge was not an option due to the destructive winds. Therefore, building a tunnel under the water was the safest and most incredible option. In 1988, after about 25 years of construction, Japan opened the Seikan Tunnel. It is the deepest operational railway tunnel in the world. It spans almost 54 km and runs about 100 m below the seabed (240 m below sea level). Its 23.3 km undersea section was the longest of any tunnel until the Channel Tunnel between the UK and France (37.9 km undersea) opened in 1994. passages.text: Underwater tunnel An underwater tunnel is a tunnel which is partly or wholly constructed under the sea or a river. They are often used where building a bridge or operating a ferry link is unviable, or to provide competition or relief for existing bridges or ferry links.[1] While short tunnels are often road tunnels which may admit motorized traffic, unmotorized traffic or both, concerns with ventilation lead to the longest tunnels (such as the Channel Tunnel or the Seikan Tunnel) being electrified rail tunnels. Types of tunnel [edit] Various methods are used to construct underwater tunnels, including an immersed tube and a submerged floating tunnel. The immersed tube method involves steel tube segments that are positioned in a trench in the sea floor and joined together. The trench is then covered and the water pumped from the tunnel.[2] Submerged floating tunnels use the law of buoyancy to remain submerged, with the tunnel attached to the sea bed by columns or tethers, or hung from pontoons on the surface.[3] Advantages [edit] Compared with bridges [edit] One such advantage would be that a tunnel would still allow shipping to pass. passages.text: Prefer Tight, Low-Permeability Ground Permeability describes how easily water can pass through soil or rock. A highly permeable formation, such as coarse gravel, can allow groundwater to flow relatively freely. In contrast, dense clay or certain types of unfractured rock may have much lower permeability. For an underwater tunnel, low-permeability ground can reduce the amount of water entering the excavation. This makes it easier to maintain a controlled working environment and reduces the demands on pumping, groundwater control and waterproofing systems. The surrounding ground also contributes to tunnel stability by transferring loads around the excavated opening. However, its strength and behaviour must be evaluated carefully. A low-permeability layer is not automatically suitable for tunnelling. Engineers must also consider rock strength, deformation, faulting, swelling, squeezing behaviour and the possibility of water-bearing fractures. A strong but heavily fractured rock formation may still create serious groundwater problems. How a Tunnel Boring Machine Works Many modern underwater tunnels are excavated using a tunnel boring machine, commonly called a TBM. A TBM is a large mechanical system with a rotating cutterhead at the front. The cutterhead breaks or cuts the surrounding soil and rock as the machine advances. Excavated material is transported away through conveyors,

The cutterhead breaks or cuts the surrounding soil and rock as the machine advances. Excavated material is transported away through conveyors, screw conveyors or other removal systems, depending on the machine type and ground conditions. Behind the cutterhead, the machine contains equipment for installing the tunnel lining. In many soft-ground and mixed-ground tunnels, precast concrete segments are assembled inside the TBM to form a strong circular lining. These segments are connected using bolts, gaskets and other specified joint systems. The lining supports the surrounding ground and provides a controlled internal surface for the finished tunnel. The annular space between the lining and the excavated ground may be filled with grout to improve contact and limit ground movement. This helps prevent voids from developing around the tunnel. The TBM advances in repeated stages: excavating the ground, removing the material, installing the lining and moving forward. The exact sequence depends on the machine design and the geological conditions. How TBMs Control Groundwater Pressure One of the biggest challenges in underwater tunnelling is groundwater pressure. However, while the preferred method of building a tunnel relies on convenience, the speed of construction, and expenditure, the most important factor remains the nature of the soil that must be penetrated. As a result, no technique can be crowned to be the absolute best. How Do Underwater Tunnels Keep The Water Out? This is the question that nags everyone the first time they drive or ride beneath a river. If there is an entire sea or river pressing down from above, why doesn't the water simply find a crack and pour in? The reassuring answer is that no underwater tunnel relies on luck. Every method above is really a method for keeping water on the outside, and each does it differently. For a bored tunnel through soft, waterlogged ground, the trick happens at the cutting face. Modern tunnel boring machines are pressurised-face machines. A slurry shield floods the sealed chamber behind the cutterhead with pressurised bentonite (a clay-and-water mix). Disadvantages [edit] Compared with bridges [edit] Tunnels can require higher costs of security and construction than bridges, but this depends on the clearance needed for ships and the water depth. This may mean that over short distances bridges may be preferred rather than tunnels (for example Dartford Crossing). Compared with ferry links [edit] As with bridges, ferry links are far cheaper to construct than tunnels, but not to operate. Also tunnels don't have the flexibility to be deployed over different routes as transport demand changes over time. Without the cost of a new ferry, the route over which a ferry provides transport can easily be changed. However, this flexibility can be a downside for customers who have come to rely on the ferry service only to see it abandoned. Fixed infrastructure such as bridges or tunnels represent a much more concrete commitment to sustained service. How TBMs Control Groundwater Pressure One of the biggest challenges in underwater tunnelling is groundwater pressure. Water surrounding the tunnel can exert significant pressure on the excavation face and the completed lining. For water at rest, the approximate hydrostatic pressure is: p = ρgh Here, p is water pressure, ρ is the density of water, g is gravitational acceleration and h is the vertical water head above the point being considered. For example, using freshwater with a density of approximately 1,000 kg/m³ and a water head of 45 m: p = 1,000 × 9.81 × 45 p = 441,450 Pa p ≈ 441 kPa This illustrates how substantial water pressure can become with increasing depth. Actual pressure conditions depend on groundwater levels, seabed elevation, soil layers, drainage and local hydraulic conditions. Pressurized-face TBMs are used in many difficult ground conditions. Earth Pressure Balance machines use conditioned excavated material to help maintain pressure at the excavation face. Slurry Shield machines use pressurized slurry to support the face and transport excavated material. Maintaining the correct face pressure is essential. If pressure is too low, the ground may

Its 1,387 m immersed-tube section, assembled from 11 segments, reaches about 60 m below sea level, making it the deepest immersed-tube tunnel in the world, all of it sitting in an active earthquake zone. - The Øresund tunnel (Denmark to Sweden, opened 2000) is one of the world's longest immersed road-and-rail tunnels. Its 3.5 km immersed section was built from 20 enormous concrete elements, each weighing tens of thousands of tonnes, before being sunk into a dredged trench. Method 2: Immersed Tube Tunnels Another major method is the immersed tube tunnel. Unlike a bored tunnel, this method uses large tunnel sections manufactured separately and then installed in a prepared trench beneath the water. Immersed tube tunnels are often suitable for relatively shallow water crossings where the seabed or riverbed can be dredged and the tunnel sections can be transported into position. The method begins by constructing large watertight tunnel elements in a dry dock or purpose-built casting facility. These elements are usually made from reinforced concrete, although steel or composite arrangements may also be used. Each section is designed to float or be transported into position. Temporary watertight bulkheads seal its ends during transport and installation.
